paras: Critic A. Walking through the independent exhibition of 1874 today, it is hard to believe that anyone found it shocking. Yet contemporary reviews were brutal. Painted outdoors and at speed, the canvases struck many critics as unfinished sketches, and one reviewer derided a small harbor scene by suggesting that an impression was all its painter had managed. What offended was not immorality but handling: visible brushwork, ordinary subjects and a refusal to hide the act of painting. Some visitors laughed openly in front of the canvases; others, more quietly, returned several times. Reproduced today on everything from calendars to umbrellas, the same pictures seem almost too agreeable to have caused offense. That this exhibition now looks charming is the surest sign of how completely it changed the way we see, and of how thoroughly its lessons have been absorbed by our eyes.

Critic B. It has become fashionable to describe Impressionism as a rupture, a clean break with centuries of academic painting. The story is appealing, and largely misleading. Landscape painters had worked outdoors for decades, and several of the supposedly radical techniques had long been used in preparatory oil sketches. What changed in the 1870s was less the method than its status: the sketch, once a private tool, was presented as a finished work. The paintings did not introduce a new way of looking so much as a new willingness to exhibit a way of looking that artists had kept to themselves. Seen in that light, the movement looks less like a revolution than an audacious change of permission. That change mattered enormously, but it deserves to be described accurately, not inflated into a myth of sudden genius.

Critic C. The more interesting question is not what the Impressionists overturned but what they made possible. Having freed the brushstroke from description, they left later painters with a problem and an opportunity. If a stroke of paint no longer had to disappear into a convincing surface, what else could it do? It is this question, rather than any single painting, that links the harbors of the 1870s to the flattened, fractured canvases of the early twentieth century. Painters who followed, many of whom rejected Impressionism quite openly, still worked inside the space it had opened. Some made the stroke heavier and more structural; others made color expressive rather than descriptive. The Impressionists were not the first modernists, but they were arguably their most important precursors, and the debt was acknowledged even by those who most wanted to escape it.

Critic D. Accounts of modern art tend to be told as a lineage of heroes, each pointing the way to the next, and the Impressionists usually appear near the beginning of the line. Such accounts are easy to teach and easy to remember. They also leave out a great deal. Several women exhibited with the group, among them Berthe Morisot, whose rapid, feathery brushwork was admired by colleagues and largely forgotten by later historians. The canon that now places certain names at the center is itself the product of later choices, and its current reappraisal suggests that the story of the movement is still being written, as much by museums as by the painters themselves. Exhibitions devoted to overlooked members of the group now draw large crowds, and each one quietly revises the lineage that textbooks once presented as settled.

items.situation: Compress: "The painting was exhibited in 1874. It gave the movement its name."
tips: Exhibited in 1874, the painting gave the movement its name.
Past participle for a passive idea, same subject.

items.situation: Compress: "Monet worked outdoors. He painted the same haystacks in different light."
tips: Working outdoors, Monet painted the same haystacks in different light.
Present participle for an active, simultaneous idea.

items.situation: Compress: "The critics had mocked the painters. They later bought their work."
tips: Having mocked the painters, the critics later bought their work.
Having + past participle for the earlier action.

items.situation: Apply ellipsis: "Morisot painted her sister, and Degas painted dancers."
tips: Morisot painted her sister; Degas, dancers.
Delete the repeated verb in the second clause.

items.situation: Fix the dangling participle: "Looking at the canvas, the colors seemed to move."
tips: Looking at the canvas, I felt the colors move.
The participle needs a subject that can actually look.

items.situation: Use a word from today in a compressed sentence about Morisot.
tips: Largely forgotten after her death, Morisot is now the subject of a reappraisal.
Past participle clause plus reappraisal or canon.

listenings.text: If you look at this small harbor scene, you are looking at the painting that accidentally named a movement. In 1874 a group of painters, tired of being judged by the official Salon, organized an independent exhibition in Paris, in the former studio of a well-known photographer. This canvas was hanging there, with a simple title that mentioned an impression of a sunrise. One critic seized on that word. Writing a mocking review, he suggested that an impression was all the painter had managed, since a finished painting was clearly beyond him, and he called the whole group Impressionists. The insult stuck, and within a few years the painters were using it themselves. Now, before we move on, I want you to do something. Walk right up to the canvas, as close as the line on the floor allows, and look at the water. You will see separate, loose strokes that do not describe anything. Then step back five or six paces, slowly. Watch the strokes turn back into a harbor, a few boats and a rising orange sun.

Last week we saw the Impressionists. Today, the long road that followed, and I want to start with a warning. The story of modern art is usually told far too neatly, as a straight line of heroes, each artist handing a torch to the next until we arrive at abstraction. It did not happen like that. Many paths were tried and abandoned, and several of the people who tried them have only recently returned to the textbooks. What later painters really took from the Impressionists was a kind of freedom: the visible brushstroke, and the right to paint ordinary modern life. What they rejected, quite quickly, was the idea that a painting should record a passing moment of light. They wanted something more solid, or more personal, or more structured. And underneath all of it runs what I like to call the quiet revolution, which is flatness. Gradually, painters stopped pretending that the canvas was a window onto a deep space, and they accepted it for what it had always been: a flat surface covered with paint.
